segments.narration: A medieval skull fooled British science for forty-one years. Piltdown, East Sussex. Announced to the Geological Society in December 1912.
They named it Eoanthropus dawsoni. Dawson's dawn-man. Half a million years old, they said, and the missing link happened to be English.
It confirmed exactly what everyone already believed: big brain first. So real African fossils got shelved for decades, because a forgery outranked them.
Then in 1953, fluorine testing broke it apart. Human skull. Orangutan jaw. Chimpanzee teeth, filed flat and stained with iron to match.
A 2016 study traced both Piltdown sites to one orangutan and one man: Charles Dawson, the amateur who found it. Forty years of textbooks, built on a fake.

verdicts.claim: The Piltdown fossils were announced at the Geological Society of London on 18 December 1912 and were not exposed as fakes until 1953, forty-one years later.

verdicts.claim: Arthur Smith Woodward named the specimen Eoanthropus dawsoni and estimated it at about 500,000 years old, presenting it as a missing link.
verdicts.note: 79% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 1 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Piltdown Man fitted the then-popular view that a large brain evolved first, and genuine finds such as Raymond Dart's Taung Child were initially overlooked because of it.
verdicts.note: 80% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: Fluorine absorption dating exposed the forgery: a medieval human skull, an orangutan lower jaw and chimpanzee teeth, file-marked and stained with iron solution and chromic acid.
verdicts.note: 79% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: A 2016 study combining morphology and DNA concluded one person made the specimens, most likely Charles Dawson, with teeth from both Piltdown sites coming from the same orangutan.
verdicts.note: 85% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 1 number(s)
